idiom_name: predicate function pointer + void *context, filtering into a caller-owned array (qsort_r-style)
implementation_notes: C has neither closures nor generics, so the filterer is written out: a predicate type whose context travels explicitly - int (*keep)(const void *elem, void *ctx), the same shape the standard library uses to inject behaviour into qsort(3), and the qsort_r(3)/bsearch_s context argument is the precedent for parameterised criteria - plus a filtering routine that copies the surviving elements into a caller-owned array. The container's own type is preserved by convention: the routine returns a count (or a new struct by value) and the caller constructs the filtered container, or the container struct carries a filterer entry in its function table. What replaces the classic structure is the type-erased void * convention - it is why predicates must carry their parameters in a context struct rather than capturing them - and nothing in the standard library provides a generic filter, so the loop is the realization.
pitfalls: The context pointer must outlive the call and stay stable: a predicate that stores or returns a pointer to a stack-allocated context makes the next call read garbage, and nothing in the type system prevents it.

A predicate that needs no context but reads a global is not re-entrant or thread-safe - the exact problem the context argument exists to avoid - so pass criteria state through ctx even for the simple cases.

The filtered result must be copied out; returning a pointer into the source array (or reusing the same buffer in place) breaks the 'filtered copy of the container' contract and corrupts the source when both are used afterwards.
Element count and capacity are unchecked: overrunning cap, computing element addresses with a wrong width, or passing a NULL predicate is undefined behaviour the compiler cannot catch.
